lesson.title: A Territory at War: Bleeding Kansas
lesson.summary: Between 1854 and 1861, proslavery and antislavery settlers fought a low grade civil war over Kansas's future, turning the territory into a violent preview of the national conflict to come.
lesson.body:
The Kansas Nebraska Act's promise that settlers themselves would decide slavery's fate in the new territory turned Kansas into a prize both sides raced to win before a single vote was even cast. Proslavery Missourians, many of them living just across the border, aimed to settle Kansas or simply show up to vote in its elections, while northern abolitionists organized through groups like the New England Emigrant Aid Company to send antislavery settlers west, founding the town of Lawrence as a free state stronghold in 1854.

The contest turned openly fraudulent almost immediately. In the March 1855 election for Kansas's first territorial legislature, thousands of proslavery Missourians, soon nicknamed Border Ruffians, crossed into Kansas for the day, voted illegally, and went home, producing a legislature that then passed a harsh slave code and outlawed even speaking against slavery. Free state settlers refused to recognize this government as legitimate and set up a rival government of their own under the unrecognized Topeka Constitution, leaving Kansas with two competing governments and no agreed authority to enforce order.

Violence followed quickly. On May 21, 1856, a large proslavery posse marched on Lawrence, burned the Free State Hotel, destroyed two antislavery printing presses, and looted the town in what became known as the Sack of Lawrence. Three days later, the militant abolitionist John Brown led a small band, including several of his sons, in a night raid along Pottawatomie Creek, dragging five proslavery settlers from their homes and killing them in an act of direct retaliation. Sporadic guerrilla fighting between proslavery and free state militias continued across the territory for years afterward, leaving a death toll historians usually estimate at several dozen to around two hundred.

The conflict reached directly into the United States Senate. On May 19 and 20, 1856, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts delivered a scathing speech titled The Crime Against Kansas, in which he mocked South Carolina Senator Andrew Butler in personal terms. Two days later, Butler's cousin, Congressman Preston Brooks, walked onto the Senate floor and beat Sumner nearly senseless with a cane, an attack so severe that Sumner needed years to recover and could barely return to full Senate duties. Northerners were horrified by the assault, while many southerners celebrated Brooks and sent him replacement canes, a split reaction that showed how far apart the sections had already drifted in their basic sense of right and wrong.

The struggle over Kansas dragged on for years afterward, most notably in the fight over the proslavery Lecompton Constitution, which President James Buchanan tried to push through Congress in 1857 despite clear evidence that the process behind it had been rigged. Kansas voters ultimately rejected the Lecompton Constitution in 1858, and the territory was not admitted to the Union until January 1861, as a free state, by which time several southern states had already begun seceding rather than accept a Union so clearly turning against slavery's expansion.
